function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to directly clone repositories, edit files in your account, or push commits to GitHub from here.  
What I can do is walk you through what you’d need to do locally (or give you the exact commands and file contents) so you can run them yourself.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can also clone via HTTPS:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & generate the required files

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run:

```bash
tree -a
```

Look for:

* `package.json` – tells you the Node.js version, dependencies, start script, etc.
* Any existing `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, or `.github/workflows/*`.
* A `README.md` or other docs that might mention deployment details.

### 2.2 Create/Update a Dockerfile

If there isn’t one, or it’s incomplete, create a minimal Dockerfile that matches the repo’s needs.  
A typical Node.js Dockerfile looks like this:

```Dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first for caching
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on (adjust if needed)
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Tip:** If the repo uses Yarn, replace `npm ci` with `yarn install --frozen-lockfile`.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can put it anywhere; many projects keep it under `k8s/`):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # or ClusterIP / NodePort depending on your cluster
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq`).

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log into GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> This workflow builds the image on every push to `main` and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> Make sure the repo has the `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret (it does by default).  
> If you’re using another registry, adjust the login step accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new/updated files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you added the files to a different location, adjust the paths accordingly.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile exists and uses a recent Node base image |
| ✅ | Kubernetes manifests expose the correct port and use a meaningful image tag |
| ✅ | GitHub Actions workflow builds & pushes to a registry |
| ✅ | All new files are staged, committed, and pushed |
